vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{A Complete Tour of SMSD}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.2,
  fig.align = "center"
)
library(SMSD)

# The cached verification study, loaded here so that the text can quote it
# from the first section on. It is loaded again, visibly, where the study is
# presented.
sim <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "aipe_simulation_results.rds",
                           package = "SMSD"))
s <- sim[["summary"]]
meta <- sim[["meta"]]

# One row of the study's summary.
pick <- function(method, distribution, true_value, width) {
  hit <- s[["method"]] == method & s[["distribution"]] == distribution &
    abs(s[["true_value"]] - true_value) < 1e-8 &
    abs(s[["width"]] - width) < 1e-8
  stopifnot(sum(hit) == 1L)
  s[hit, ]
}
smd_row <- function(true_value, distribution = "normal") {
  pick("Standardized mean difference", distribution, true_value, 0.40)
}
cor_row <- function(true_value, width, distribution = "normal") {
  pick("Pearson correlation", distribution, true_value, width)
}

# Display helpers. Stored values are never rounded; these format for text.
f <- function(x, digits = 3) {
  formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ",")
}
value_of <- function(check, term) {
  check[["value"]][check[["term"]] == term]
}
limits_of <- function(check, digits = 3) {
  paste0("[", f(value_of(check, "lower_limit"), digits), ", ",
         f(value_of(check, "upper_limit"), digits), "]")
}
# "contains" or "does not contain", for a sentence about an interval and
# the value used to generate the data.
contains <- function(check, truth) {
  inside <- value_of(check, "lower_limit") <= truth &&
    truth <= value_of(check, "upper_limit")
  if (inside) "contains" else "does not contain"
}
G_text <- f(meta[["G"]], 0)

# The designs of the method sections, each simulated with its sensitivity
# function and cached in the same file.
tour <- sim[["tour"]]
tour_value <- function(design, term) {
  rows <- tour[["summary"]]
  hit <- rows[["design"]] == design & rows[["term"]] == term
  stopifnot(sum(hit) == 1L)
  rows[["value"]][hit]
}
tour_G_text <- f(tour[["G"]], 0)
```

## Why Sequential Design

Planning a sample size ordinarily requires the very quantities the study
is meant to estimate. A sample size for a target power needs the effect
size. A sample size for a confidence interval of a target width needs the
sampling variance of the estimator, which for most effect sizes depends on
the effect size itself and on the shape of the distribution of the data.
When the planning values are wrong, the study is too small for its purpose
or larger than it needed to be (Maxwell, Kelley, & Rausch, 2008).

Accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) plans a study around the width of
the confidence interval rather than the outcome of a significance test:
the aim is an interval no wider than a value ω that the researcher judges
informative (Kelley, 2007a, 2008; Kelley & Lai, 2011; Kelley & Maxwell,
2003; Kelley & Rausch, 2006). The fixed sample size form of AIPE, in which
the sample size follows from planning values, is in the companion package
`DMAR`, the successor to `MBESS` (Kelley, 2007b).

`SMSD` ("Sequential Methods for Study Design") is for the case in which no
trustworthy planning value exists. Data are collected in stages, and a
stopping rule computed from the data in hand says when there are enough.
The package has four families of procedures.

* **Sequential AIPE** (`seq_aipe_*()`): a confidence interval no wider
  than ω for the standardized mean difference, the coefficient of
  variation, the standardized mean, the regression slope, and a contrast
  of means (Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay, 2018); for Pearson's
  correlation, Kendall's tau, Spearman's rho, and the squared multiple
  correlation (Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay, 2019); and for the Gini
  index (Chattopadhyay & De, 2016).
* **Minimum risk point estimation** (`seq_mr_cv()`, `seq_mr_smd()`): the
  sample size that minimizes the cost of estimation error plus the cost of
  sampling (Chattopadhyay & Kelley, 2016, 2017).
* **A budget constrained procedure** (`seq_budget()`): a contrast of
  several population means estimated as precisely as a fixed budget
  allows when an observation costs a different amount in each population
  (Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, & Padalunkal, 2025).
* **Classical procedures** for a mean, the location of a negative
  exponential distribution, or a median (`seq_fwd_*()`, `seq_mr_*_mean()`,
  `seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb()`, `seq_br_norm_mean()`, `ts_*()`,
  `seq_blci_dfr_median()`), from the two stage and purely sequential
  tradition of Stein (1945), Anscombe (1953), Robbins (1959), and Chow and
  Robbins (1965), as collected by Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009).

This vignette goes through all four with code that runs, in the order in
which a user calls the functions. It ends with a Monte Carlo study of two
of the procedures, `r G_text` replications per condition, computed once
and stored in the package, that shows where the intervals can be trusted
and where they cannot. The same cached file holds several thousand
simulated studies of the design of each example, so every section can say
how its own design behaves in the long run.

## The Shared Engine

The `seq_aipe_*()` procedures are built from the same three pieces. (The
squared multiple correlation, Method 3 below, has the same structure with
a pilot rule and correction terms of its own.) Write ω for the target full
width of the confidence interval (the argument `width`: the upper limit
minus the lower limit), *z* for the standard normal quantile of the
confidence level (1.96 at 95%), and ξ<sup>2</sup> for the asymptotic
variance of the estimator, that is, the limit of *n* times its sampling
variance.

**A pilot sample size.** Before any data exist, only ω and the confidence
level are known. The first check is made at

> *m* = max{ *m*<sub>0</sub>, ⌈2*z* / ω⌉ }

observations (per group, in a design with groups), where ⌈ ⌉ rounds up and
*m*<sub>0</sub> is a minimum, 4 by default (Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay,
2018, Equation 21; 2019, Equation 9). Each `seq_aipe_*_pilot()` function
returns this number.

**A stopping rule.** At the pilot sample size and after every addition,
sampling stops at the first *n* for which

> *n* ≥ (2*z* / ω)<sup>2</sup> × (the estimate of ξ<sup>2</sup> + 1/*n*)

(2018, Equation 22; 2019, Equation 10). The estimate of ξ<sup>2</sup> is
computed from the data in hand without assuming a distribution, and 1/*n*
is a correction that keeps the rule from being met too early. The quantity
on the right, rounded up, is the row `criterion_n` of every check.

**A confidence interval.** At the stopping point the interval is

> the estimate ± *z* × √(the estimate of ξ<sup>2</sup> / *n*)

(2018, Equation 23; 2019, Equation 11), symmetric about the estimate on
the scale of the effect size.

### Two Guarantees of Different Kinds

The width is guaranteed. Whenever the rule is met the interval is no wider
than ω, in every sample, because the rule is the width requirement solved
for *n*.

The coverage is not guaranteed at any particular width. The articles prove
that the probability that the interval contains the population value
approaches the confidence level as ω shrinks, and so as the final sample
grows (2018, p. 232; 2019, p. 495). How close it is at a width a researcher
might choose depends on the effect size and on its true value. For some
effect sizes it is at the confidence level already at wide targets; for
others it falls well short. Each section below says which, with the
measured figure, and the study at the end shows the pattern in detail for
two effect sizes.

### When the Variance Estimate Is Not Yet Usable

Several of the variance estimators are differences of moment terms, and in
a small sample they can come out zero or negative. The articles bound the
estimate below by *n*<sup>−3</sup> (2018, Equation 27; 2019, Equation 8,
which has *n*<sup>−γ</sup> and is used with γ = 3 throughout, p. 494), and
the 2019 article calls a negative estimate a chance that is positive "even
though negligible" (p. 494). At small pilot sample sizes
it is not negligible: in the study at the end of this vignette, the
estimate was zero or negative at one or more checks in
`r f(cor_row(0.7, 0.30)$pct_variance_unusable, 1)`% of the studies of a
correlation of 0.7 at a target width of 0.30. Under the rule as printed,
the bound would stand in for such an estimate and sampling would end at
once with an interval far narrower than the data support.

The package departs from the printed rule here, deliberately. When the raw
variance estimate is zero, negative, or not finite, no variance has been
estimated: the check reports the stopping rule as **not met**, the
confidence limits are `NA`, `criterion_n` is at least one more than the
current sample size, the attribute `variance_unusable` is `TRUE`, and a
note says why. Sampling continues. A positive estimate, however small, is
used as the articles prescribe (the larger of it and *n*<sup>−3</sup>).

A pilot sample of ten pairs with a true correlation of 0.8 shows what such
a check looks like.

```{r unusable}
set.seed(113)
m <- seq_aipe_r_pilot(width = 0.40)
x <- rnorm(m)
y <- 0.8 * x + 0.6 * rnorm(m)
seq_aipe_r(x, y, width = 0.40)
```

The remedy is the one the note gives: collect more data and check again.
A loop written on `attr(out, "is_satisfied")` does that without any
special handling.

### The Single Call Contract

A sequential study runs over weeks or months, but no function in the
package waits, prompts, or keeps state. For a procedure `seq_X`:

* `seq_X_pilot()` returns the pilot sample size, an integer.
* `seq_X()` takes all the data collected so far, evaluates the stopping
  rule once, and returns an object of class `smsd_check`: a data frame
  with columns `term` and `value`, with the decision in
  `attr(out, "is_satisfied")`, which is always `TRUE` or `FALSE`. The user
  calls it again whenever more data are in.
* `print()`, `summary()`, and `as.data.frame()` methods, and `tidy()` and
  `glance()` methods for the generics of the `generics` package, present
  the object; the stored values are never rounded.
* `seq_path()` applies a check function to data in hand at every
  successive sample size and returns the whole path, with a `plot()`
  method.
* `seq_report()` writes the paragraph for a methods section.
* `seq_X_sensitivity()` simulates the whole procedure before any data are
  collected. Every `seq_aipe_*()` procedure, both minimum risk procedures,
  and the budget constrained procedure have one. (For the correlation it
  simulates the Pearson coefficient only; the measured coverage of the
  Kendall and Spearman intervals is on the help page of `seq_aipe_r()`.)

## Method 1: The Standardized Mean Difference, Step by Step

The standardized mean difference is δ = (μ<sub>1</sub> − μ<sub>2</sub>) / σ,
the difference between two population means in units of their common
standard deviation (Cohen, 1988; Kelley & Rausch, 2006). Its sequential
AIPE procedure is developed in detail by Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay
(2018).

A human resources team introduces a training program and compares the
engagement ratings (on a 1 to 7 scale) of trained employees with those of
a control group. They want a 95% confidence interval for δ no wider than
ω = 0.40. They do not know δ, so they cannot fix the sample size honestly
in advance. In this illustration the data are simulated with means 4.9 and
4.5 and a standard deviation of 0.8 in both groups, so the true value is
δ = 0.4 / 0.8 = 0.5.

First, the pilot sample size, and the first check on that many employees
per group.

```{r smd-pilot}
set.seed(113)
width <- 0.40
m <- seq_aipe_smd_pilot(width = width)
m

new_ratings <- function(k, mean) rnorm(k, mean = mean, sd = 0.8)
trained <- new_ratings(m, 4.9)
control <- new_ratings(m, 4.5)

out <- seq_aipe_smd(trained, control, width = width)
out
```

The check reports the estimate and its interval, the variance estimate
(`xi_squared`), the sample size per group that the rule currently requires
(`criterion_n`), and the decision. With `r attr(out, "current_n")` per
group against a criterion of `r attr(out, "criterion_n")`, the rule is not
met. The team adds one employee to each group and checks again, until it
is. This loop is the whole of a sequential study: collect, check, and stop
at the first check that is met.

```{r smd-loop}
while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {
  trained <- c(trained, new_ratings(1, 4.9))
  control <- c(control, new_ratings(1, 4.5))
  out <- seq_aipe_smd(trained, control, width = width)
}
out
```

The rule is met at `r attr(out, "current_n")` employees per group. The
interval, `r limits_of(out)`, is
`r f(value_of(out, "upper_limit") - value_of(out, "lower_limit"))` wide,
within the target of `r width`, and it `r contains(out, 0.5)` the value
used to generate the data, 0.5. The team never supplied a guess of δ or of
the shape of the ratings.

The object is an ordinary data frame underneath, and its methods return
what further computation needs.

```{r smd-methods}
summary(out)
generics::tidy(out)
out$value[out$term == "smd"]
```

### The Path and the Report

`seq_path()` applies the same check to data in hand at every sample size
from the pilot on. For the data just collected it returns the path the
study followed, and `plot()` draws it: the interval narrowing toward its
target width, and the current sample size meeting the criterion.

```{r smd-path, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Two stacked panels. Top: the estimated standardized mean difference with its confidence interval against the sample size per group; the interval narrows until its width reaches the target. Bottom: the current sample size and the criterion sample size against the sample size per group; the two lines meet at the stopping point."}
path <- seq_path(seq_aipe_smd, list(group_1 = trained, group_2 = control),
                 width = width)
plot(path)
```

`seq_report()` turns a check or a path into the paragraph a methods
section needs, with the reference for the procedure.

```{r smd-report}
seq_report(path)
```

### The Correction to Equation 26

For this effect size the variance estimator is the one under Equation 27
of the 2018 article, with one correction. Equation 26 as printed, and its
sample version, omit a factor of 1/2 in the term that carries the third
central moments of the two groups. The package implements the corrected
variance. The two forms differ only when the groups differ both in their
means and in their third central moments; for groups of the same shape
they agree. The authors' correction is posted at
<https://kenkelley.org/wp-content/uploads/articles/Kelley_Darku_Chattopadhyay_Equation_26.pdf>
and is installed with the package:

```{r eq26}
file.exists(system.file("eq26_correction.pdf", package = "SMSD"))
```

### How Far to Trust the Interval

For the standardized mean difference the asymptotic guarantee is already
good at this width. In the verification study at the end of this vignette,
the design used here (δ = 0.5, ω = 0.40, normal data) covered δ in
`r f(100 * smd_row(0.5)$coverage, 1)`% of `r G_text` simulated studies,
with a mean final sample size of `r f(smd_row(0.5)$mean_n, 1)` per group.
With right skewed data in both groups the figure was
`r f(100 * smd_row(0.5, "skewed")$coverage, 1)`%.

## Method 2: Correlation Coefficients

Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2019) give the sequential AIPE procedure
for a population correlation: Pearson's product moment correlation, with a
variance estimator built on the joint central moments of the two variables
(their Equation 3 rests on Lee, 1990), and Kendall's tau and Spearman's
rho, with rank based estimators. The `method` argument of `seq_aipe_r()`
selects the coefficient.

An information systems researcher relates time on task to a usability
rating across users and wants a 95% interval for the correlation no wider
than ω = 0.15. The pairs below are simulated, in the order in which they
would be observed, from a bivariate normal distribution with ρ = 0.5.

```{r cor-data}
set.seed(113)
rho <- 0.5
time_on_task <- rnorm(600)
usability <- rho * time_on_task + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(600)

m <- seq_aipe_r_pilot(width = 0.15)
m
pilot_check <- seq_aipe_r(time_on_task[1:m], usability[1:m], width = 0.15)
pilot_check
```

The rule is not met at the pilot. The check also shows how unsettled the
variance estimate is in a small sample: `xi_squared` is
`r f(value_of(pilot_check, "xi_squared"))`, where the population value for
bivariate normal data is (1 − ρ<sup>2</sup>)<sup>2</sup> = 0.5625, and
`criterion_n` moves with it. Rather than add one pair at a time by hand,
`seq_path()` evaluates the rule at every sample size from the pilot on.
The data go in one list, named after the data arguments of the check
function, so that every stage sees only the pairs observed up to that
point.

```{r cor-path}
path_r <- seq_path(seq_aipe_r, list(x = time_on_task, y = usability),
                   width = 0.15)
path_r
```

```{r cor-plot, fig.alt = "The estimated correlation with its confidence interval against the number of pairs. The interval narrows as pairs are added; the stopping point is marked, and the stages after it are drawn in gray."}
plot(path_r, which = "estimate")
```

The estimate to report is the one at the first sample size at which the
rule was met, *n* = `r attr(path_r, "stop_n")`:
*r* = `r f(value_of(attr(path_r, "final_check"), "r"))`, 95% CI
`r limits_of(attr(path_r, "final_check"))`, which
`r contains(attr(path_r, "final_check"), 0.5)` ρ = 0.5. The rows after
that point, drawn in gray, show what the rule would have said had sampling
continued. They are not grounds for choosing a later stopping point: the
width and coverage properties belong to the first sample size at which the
rule is met.

The same pairs can be analyzed with a rank based coefficient. Each
coefficient estimates its own population value (for bivariate normal data
with ρ = 0.5, Kendall's tau is 1/3 and Spearman's rho is 0.483) and has
its own variance estimator, so each has its own criterion.

```{r cor-rank}
c(kendall = 2 / pi * asin(rho), spearman = 6 / pi * asin(rho / 2))

n_r <- attr(path_r, "stop_n")
kendall <- seq_aipe_r(time_on_task[1:n_r], usability[1:n_r], width = 0.15,
                      method = "kendall")
spearman <- seq_aipe_r(time_on_task[1:n_r], usability[1:n_r], width = 0.15,
                       method = "spearman")
rbind(kendall = summary(kendall), spearman = summary(spearman))[
  , c("estimate", "lower_limit", "upper_limit", "current_n", "criterion_n",
      "is_satisfied")]
```

These two checks are made at the Pearson stopping point, to set the three
criteria side by side; they are not where a study of either rank based
coefficient would stop. The coefficient is chosen before the data are
collected, and a study that will report Kendall's tau or Spearman's rho
runs its own path with that `method` from the pilot sample on and stops
at the first sample size at which its own rule is met.

### How Far to Trust a Correlation Interval

The correlation is the effect size for which the asymptotic guarantee
needs the most care, and Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2019) say so:
their Table 2 (p. 498) reports coverage of .90 for a 95% interval of width
0.2 when ρ = .5. A wide target stops the procedure in a small sample, where
the variance estimate tends to run low. A strong correlation makes it
worse, because its interval is short and the rule can be met with few
pairs. In the verification study (normal data, 95%), the design used here,
ρ = 0.5 at ω = 0.15, covered ρ in
`r f(100 * cor_row(0.5, 0.15)$coverage, 1)`% of studies; at ω = 0.30 the
figure was `r f(100 * cor_row(0.5, 0.30)$coverage, 1)`%, and for ρ = 0.7 at
ω = 0.30 it was `r f(100 * cor_row(0.7, 0.30)$coverage, 1)`%. At ω = 0.08
coverage was `r f(100 * cor_row(0.5, 0.08)$coverage, 1)`% for ρ = 0.5 and
`r f(100 * cor_row(0.7, 0.08)$coverage, 1)`% for ρ = 0.7.

The help page of `seq_aipe_r_sensitivity()` reports a stronger case still:
for ρ = 0.9, coverage of 0.45 at a width of 0.1 and 0.90 only at a width of
0.025.

Kendall's tau and Spearman's rho show the same pattern, less severely.
The help page of `seq_aipe_r()` reports simulations of all three
coefficients for the same bivariate normal data and the same widths. With
ρ = 0.4, coverage at a width of 0.2 was 0.94 for both rank based
coefficients (0.93 for Pearson's), and at a width of 0.4 it was 0.91 for
Kendall's tau and 0.87 for Spearman's rho (0.78 for Pearson's). With
ρ = 0.8 or −0.8 at a width of 0.2 it was 0.91 to 0.92 for Kendall's tau
and 0.87 to 0.88 for Spearman's rho (0.69 for Pearson's with ρ = 0.8).
The rank based variance estimators assume continuous data. With tied
values (ratings on a 5 point scale, for example) they are too small, and
`seq_aipe_r()` warns.

For a correlation, then, choose a narrow target and raise the minimum
pilot sample size `m_0` of `seq_aipe_r_pilot()` when the correlation may
be strong. For Pearson's coefficient, run `seq_aipe_r_sensitivity()`,
which simulates the Pearson interval only, at the strongest correlation
that is plausible before collecting data. The rank based coefficients have
no sensitivity function; the figures above are the guide.

## Method 3: The Squared Multiple Correlation

The 2019 article extends the procedure to the population squared multiple
correlation of a regression with *p* predictors. Two things set it apart
from everything else in the family.

**It assumes multivariate normality.** The article develops it "under
multivariate normal assumption only" (p. 503), because no distribution
free interval for the squared multiple correlation was available.

**Its coverage depends on the number of predictors.** The sample value
overestimates the population value by an amount that grows with *p*
relative to *n*, the interval is built around the sample value, and the
stopping rule does not correct for it.

The functions are `seq_aipe_R2_pilot()`, which needs the number of
predictors, and `seq_aipe_R2()`, which reports the interval built on the
normal theory variance of Olkin and Finn (1995) by default
(`ci_method = "wald"`) or the interval of Bonett and Wright (2011)
(`ci_method = "log_transformed"`). The stopping rule for the default
interval is not Equation 63 of the article exactly as printed (p. 505):
the correction 1/*n* enters its last factor with the opposite sign. The
help page of `seq_aipe_R2()` gives both forms and reports that the form
the package uses, and not the printed one, reproduces the article's
Tables 13 and 14.

An organizational researcher asks how well autonomy, supervisor support,
and workload together predict job satisfaction, and wants a 95% interval
for the population squared multiple correlation no wider than ω = 0.10.
The data are simulated from a multivariate normal distribution with a
population value of 0.50.

```{r r2-data}
set.seed(113)
b <- c(0.45, 0.40, -0.30)
predictors <- cbind(autonomy = rnorm(1000), support = rnorm(1000),
                    workload = rnorm(1000))
satisfaction <- drop(predictors %*% b) + rnorm(1000, sd = sqrt(sum(b^2)))

m <- seq_aipe_R2_pilot(width = 0.10, p = 3)
m
seq_aipe_R2(predictors[1:m, ], satisfaction[1:m], width = 0.10)
```

`seq_path()` cannot work out this pilot sample size by itself, because it
depends on the number of predictors, so it is supplied as `start`.

```{r r2-path}
path_R2 <- seq_path(seq_aipe_R2, list(x = predictors, y = satisfaction),
                    width = 0.10, start = m)
attr(path_R2, "stop_n")
attr(path_R2, "final_check")
```

The interval at the stopping point, `r limits_of(attr(path_R2,
"final_check"))`, `r contains(attr(path_R2, "final_check"), 0.5)` the
population value of 0.50. In `r tour_G_text` simulated studies of this
design (three predictors, a population value of .50, ω = .10, multivariate
normal data), coverage was `r f(tour_value("R2", "coverage"), 3)`, with a
mean final sample size of `r f(tour_value("R2", "mean_n"), 0)`; the help
page of `seq_aipe_R2()` reports .946 from 40,000.

### Two Cautions

Both are documented with simulations on the help page of `seq_aipe_R2()`;
the figures here are quoted from it.

*Data that are not normal.* In the same design, coverage was .902 for a
multivariate *t* distribution with 10 degrees of freedom, .788 with 5
degrees of freedom, and .860 for right skewed predictors and errors. A
narrower target does not help, because the normal theory variance is too
small for heavy tailed data at any sample size.
<!-- figures from `?seq_aipe_R2` -->

*Many predictors.* With a population value of .50, coverage was .865 with
10 predictors and .790 with 15 at ω = .20, and .668 and .361 at ω = .30.
The chunk below shows how that happens. Twenty predictors are generated
that have nothing to do with the response, so the population value is 0.
<!-- figures from `?seq_aipe_R2` -->

```{r r2-many}
set.seed(113)
m_20 <- seq_aipe_R2_pilot(width = 0.30, p = 20)
noise <- matrix(rnorm(m_20 * 20), nrow = m_20)
unrelated <- rnorm(m_20)
many <- seq_aipe_R2(noise, unrelated, width = 0.30)
many
```

```{r r2-many-text, include = FALSE}
many_decision <- if (attr(many, "is_satisfied")) {
  "met at the very first check"
} else {
  "not yet met"
}
```

With `r m_20` observations and 20 predictors the sample value is
`r f(value_of(many, "R2"), 2)`, and the rule is
`r many_decision`,
with an interval of `r limits_of(many, 2)` for a population value of 0. The
article offers no remedy for this, and the function does not alter the
stopping rule to correct for it. It attaches the note shown, whenever an
interval is reported from fewer than *p* × max(20, 2*p*) observations,
and the help page reports that in this condition the rule was met at the
first check in 36% of simulated data sets and that the final interval
contained 0 in 4% of replications.

With many predictors or a wide target, raise `m_0` in
`seq_aipe_R2_pilot()` and run `seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity()` at the planned
width and number of predictors before relying on the procedure. When a
planning value is available, `ss_aipe_R2()` and `ci_R2()` in `DMAR` work
from the exact sampling distribution of the sample value (Kelley, 2008).

## Method 4: The Coefficient of Variation

The coefficient of variation, κ = σ / μ, expresses the standard deviation
relative to the mean and suits ratio scale outcomes such as durations and
amounts. Its sequential AIPE procedure is in Kelley, Darku, and
Chattopadhyay (2018); Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016) treat the same
estimator under a minimum risk criterion (see below).

An operations analyst studies how variable customer service times are
relative to their mean, with a target width of ω = 0.04. The times are
simulated from a gamma distribution with a mean of 10 minutes and κ = 0.2.

```{r cv}
set.seed(113)
service_time <- rgamma(400, shape = 25, scale = 0.4)

seq_aipe_cv_pilot(width = 0.04)
path_cv <- seq_path(seq_aipe_cv, service_time, width = 0.04)
attr(path_cv, "stop_n")
attr(path_cv, "final_check")
```

The interval `r contains(attr(path_cv, "final_check"), 0.2)` κ = 0.2. In
`r tour_G_text` simulated studies of this design, coverage was
`r f(tour_value("cv", "coverage"), 3)`, with a mean final sample size of
`r f(tour_value("cv", "mean_n"), 0)`. These are settings of the article's
Table 4 (p. 234), which reports coverage of .942 for normal data and .934
for gamma data with κ = .2 at ω = .04. A target that is wide relative to κ
is another matter: with κ = 0.5 the help page of `seq_aipe_cv()` reports
coverage of 0.88 for gamma data and 0.79 for lognormal data at ω = 0.2,
where the procedure stops with about 52 and 62 observations.

## Method 5: The Simple Linear Regression Slope

The slope of the regression of *y* on *x*, β<sub>1</sub>, is another
member of the 2018 class; Kelley and Maxwell (2003) give the fixed sample
size AIPE treatment of regression coefficients. Neither normal errors nor
constant error variance is assumed.

An education researcher relates the hours students study over a term to
their score on the final examination and wants a 95% interval for the
slope no wider than ω = 0.2 points per hour. The data are simulated with a
slope of 0.5, hours with a standard deviation of 6, and errors with a
standard deviation of 6.

```{r slope}
set.seed(113)
hours <- rnorm(700, mean = 40, sd = 6)
score <- 50 + 0.5 * hours + rnorm(700, sd = 6)

seq_aipe_reg_coef_pilot(width = 0.2)
path_b <- seq_path(seq_aipe_reg_coef, list(x = hours, y = score),
                   width = 0.2)
attr(path_b, "stop_n")
attr(path_b, "final_check")
```

The interval `r contains(attr(path_b, "final_check"), 0.5)` the slope of
0.5.

Two properties of this procedure need to be known before it is used.

*Units.* The slope and ω are in units of *y* per unit of *x*, while the
pilot sample size, the correction 1/*n* in the stopping rule, and the
bound *n*<sup>−3</sup> on the variance estimate are pure numbers, as
printed in the article. They play their intended roles when
ξ<sup>2</sup>, the error variance over the variance of *x*, is not many
orders of magnitude from one (here it is 6<sup>2</sup> / 6<sup>2</sup> =
1). If the two variables are recorded in very different units, rescale
one of them, and ω with it, first. The contrast of Method 7 has the same
property.

*Coverage.* In `r tour_G_text` simulated studies of the design above (a
slope of 0.5 at ω = 0.2 with ξ<sup>2</sup> = 1, normal data), coverage was
`r f(tour_value("reg_coef", "coverage"), 3)`, with a mean final sample
size of `r f(tour_value("reg_coef", "mean_n"), 0)` pairs; the variance
estimate was unusable at one or more checks in
`r f(tour_value("reg_coef", "pct_variance_unusable"), 1)`% of them. The
help page of `seq_aipe_reg_coef()` reports what a wider target does: at
ω = 0.4 coverage was 0.83 for normal data and 0.71 for right skewed data,
because in pilot samples of 10 pairs the variance estimate was zero or
negative 16% of the time for normal data, and when it is usable it tends
to run low. A larger minimum pilot sample size helps (with `m_0 = 50`,
0.92 for normal and 0.89 for skewed data at ω = 0.4). A stronger
relationship is harder, as for the correlation: the help page of
`seq_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity()` reports, for a slope of 2 with
ξ<sup>2</sup> = 1, coverage of 0.61 at ω = 0.2 and 0.87 at ω = 0.1. Run
that function for the planned design before collecting data.

## Method 6: The Standardized Mean

The standardized mean, μ / σ, is the mean in standard deviation units; for
difference scores it is the standardized mean change. It is Example 3 of
Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018). Here the gain scores of
participants in a training study are simulated with a mean of 2 and a
standard deviation of 5, so μ / σ = 0.4, and the target width is ω = 0.40.

```{r sm}
set.seed(113)
gain <- rnorm(300, mean = 2, sd = 5)

seq_aipe_sm_pilot(width = 0.40)
path_sm <- seq_path(seq_aipe_sm, gain, width = 0.40)
attr(path_sm, "stop_n")
attr(path_sm, "final_check")
```

The interval `r contains(attr(path_sm, "final_check"), 0.4)` 0.4. In
`r tour_G_text` simulated studies of this design, coverage was
`r f(tour_value("sm", "coverage"), 3)`, with a mean final sample size of
`r f(tour_value("sm", "mean_n"), 0)`. The help page of `seq_aipe_sm()`
reports that skewed data lower it at this width (0.893 for a standardized
chi square distribution with 3 degrees of freedom and μ / σ = 1) and less
so at ω = 0.2 (0.940).

## Method 7: A Contrast Among Several Groups

A contrast ψ = Σ *c*<sub>k</sub> μ<sub>k</sub> compares group means with
chosen weights (Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay, 2018, Example 6; Maxwell,
Delaney, & Kelley, 2027, treat contrasts at length). `seq_aipe_c()` takes
a list with one vector per group and the weights. The groups must be the
same size, because the published procedure adds an observation to every
group at each stage. Neither normality nor equal variances is assumed.

Three onboarding programs are compared on an engagement rating with a
standard deviation of about 1: a mentored program against the average of
an online and a classroom program, with weights (1, −1/2, −1/2). The true
means are 5.0, 4.6, and 4.4, so ψ = 5.0 − 4.5 = 0.5, and the target width
is ω = 0.40.

```{r contrast}
set.seed(113)
true_means <- c(mentored = 5.0, online = 4.6, classroom = 4.4)
weights <- c(1, -0.5, -0.5)
ratings <- lapply(true_means, function(mu) rnorm(250, mean = mu, sd = 1))

seq_aipe_c_pilot(width = 0.40)
path_c <- seq_path(seq_aipe_c, list(groups = ratings),
                   contrast_weights = weights, width = 0.40)
attr(path_c, "stop_n")
attr(path_c, "final_check")
```

The interval `r contains(attr(path_c, "final_check"), 0.5)` ψ = 0.5, with
`r attr(path_c, "stop_n")` participants in each of the three groups. In
`r tour_G_text` simulated studies of this design, coverage was
`r f(tour_value("contrast", "coverage"), 3)`, with a mean final sample
size of `r f(tour_value("contrast", "mean_n"), 0)` per group; the help
page of `seq_aipe_c()` reports 0.949 for skewed groups with unequal
variances at the same width. The variance estimate is a weighted
sum of sample variances, which cannot be negative, so the complication of
Methods 2 and 5 does not arise.

## Method 8: The Gini Index

The Gini index summarizes inequality, of incomes for example, on a scale
from 0 to 1. Its sequential fixed width procedure is due to Chattopadhyay
and De (2016). The package states the stopping rule in the form of the
rest of the family, with the full width ω as the target. The interval it
reports is the one the rest of the family reports, the estimate plus and
minus *z* times its estimated standard error, which the rule keeps within
ω; the article's interval is the estimate plus and minus ω / 2, and can
be formed from the `gini` row once the rule is met. Here incomes are
simulated from a lognormal distribution whose Gini index is 0.3, and the
target width is ω = 0.10.

```{r gini}
set.seed(113)
sdlog <- sqrt(2) * qnorm((0.3 + 1) / 2)
income <- rlnorm(300, meanlog = 10.8, sdlog = sdlog)

seq_aipe_gini_pilot(width = 0.10)
path_g <- seq_path(seq_aipe_gini, income, width = 0.10)
attr(path_g, "stop_n")
attr(path_g, "final_check")
```

The interval `r contains(attr(path_g, "final_check"), 0.3)` 0.3. Coverage
for this effect size depends on the distribution. In `r tour_G_text`
simulated studies of this design, coverage was
`r f(tour_value("gini", "coverage"), 3)`, with a mean final sample size of
`r f(tour_value("gini", "mean_n"), 0)`: a nominal 95% interval for skewed
incomes at this width covers less often than its label says. The help page
of `seq_aipe_gini()` reports 0.89 for the same distribution at ω = 0.2,
and 0.951 at ω = 0.1 for exponential data (a Gini index of 0.5). Those
figures are for the interval the function reports. Once the rule is met,
the article's interval, the estimate plus and minus ω / 2, contains that
interval, so it covers at least as often.

## Method 9: A Contrast Under a Fixed Budget

Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, and Padalunkal (2025) take up a
different constraint. A contrast of *K* population means is to be
estimated, an observation costs a different amount in each population,
and the total budget is fixed. Precision is then governed by the budget
rather than by a target width: the question is how to divide the budget
among the populations so that the contrast is estimated as precisely as
possible.

A company compares a self-paced online onboarding module with two
instructor-led formats on a certification score, for which larger is
better. An online trainee costs 20 to assess and an instructor-led trainee
40; the budget is 6,000. The contrast is the online mean minus the average
of the two instructor-led means.

If the standard deviations were known, Theorem 1 of the article (its
Equation 12) would give the best allocation directly.

```{r budget-optimal}
weights <- c(1, -0.5, -0.5)
costs <- c(online = 20, classroom = 40, workshop = 40)
budget <- 6000

seq_budget_optimal(contrast_weights = weights, sigmas = c(8, 8, 8),
                   cost_per_group = costs, budget = budget)
```

The online group, which has both the larger weight and the lower cost,
receives the most observations: the optimal size of a group is
proportional to the absolute value of its weight times its standard
deviation, divided by the square root of its cost. The standard
deviations are not known, so the article's sequential procedure
substitutes the sample standard deviations, updated as observations
arrive: a population has met its criterion when its sample size is at
least its estimated optimal size (Equation 18). `seq_budget()` evaluates
that criterion for every group on the data in hand, and
`seq_budget_next()` names the group the next observation should come
from. It names only a group whose next observation the remaining budget
can pay for, and returns `NA` when sampling has ended, so a loop written
on it cannot spend more than the budget.

The article and the package's default differ in what happens after a
group has met its criterion. In the article a population is closed the
first time it meets its criterion and is not sampled again, and the
populations still open are sampled in turn, one observation at a time
(pp. 429 to 430). A check sees only the data in hand, so by default
`seq_budget()` judges every group afresh at each check. A group that met
its criterion at an earlier check is not closed: if it is below its
criterion on the current data, because the standard deviations have
moved, it is a candidate for the next observation again. And
`seq_budget_next()` sends the next observation to the candidate furthest
below its estimated optimal size, not to the open populations in turn.
That default is the package's choice, not the article's procedure. The
article's first passage rule is an option: pass the `met_per_group`
attribute of the previous check to `seq_budget()` as `closed`, and ask
`seq_budget_next()` for `order = "rounds"`. The loop below uses the
default; the article's rule is run on the same pilot data after it.

The scores are simulated with means 74, 75, and 75 and a standard
deviation of 8, so the true contrast is −1: the online module is one point
worse. The pilot is 10 trainees per group, the size used in the article's
simulations (p. 432), and its cost comes out of the same budget.

```{r budget-run}
set.seed(113)
true_means <- c(74, 75, 75)
scores <- lapply(true_means, function(mu) {
  rnorm(seq_budget_pilot(m_0 = 10), mean = mu, sd = 8)
})

repeat {
  out <- seq_budget(scores, weights, cost_per_group = costs, budget = budget)
  g <- seq_budget_next(out)
  if (is.na(g)) break
  scores[[g]] <- c(scores[[g]], rnorm(1, mean = true_means[g], sd = 8))
}
out
attr(out, "n_per_group")
attr(out, "criterion_per_group")
```

### How Sampling Ends

The total cost is `r f(value_of(out, "current_total_cost"), 0)` against a
budget of `r f(budget, 0)`: the budget was not exceeded. The note on the
object says how sampling ended, and three attributes record it.

```{r budget-ending}
c(is_satisfied = attr(out, "is_satisfied"), rule_met = attr(out, "rule_met"),
  budget_exhausted = attr(out, "budget_exhausted"))
attr(out, "remaining_budget")
```

Sampling ends in one of two ways (the article, p. 430): every group has
met its criterion (`rule_met`), or what is left of the budget cannot pay
for another observation from a group still below its criterion
(`budget_exhausted`). `is_satisfied` is `TRUE` in either case. A check
at which sampling has ended with the current total below the criterion
total has stopped by exhaustion. That is not a failure, and the estimate
and interval it reports are the ones to use.

Which ending is the usual one depends on the reading of the procedure.
With the package's default it is exhaustion. The targets of Equation 18,
before they are rounded up to criterion sample sizes, cost exactly the
budget in total, so when every group is judged on the current data, all
of them can be at or above their criteria within the budget only if each
sample size equals its target exactly. Of `r tour_G_text` simulated
studies of this design, run with `seq_budget_sensitivity()`,
`r if (tour_value("budget", "pct_rule_met") == 0) "every one" else paste0(f(100 - tour_value("budget", "pct_rule_met"), 1), "%")`
ended by exhaustion under the default.

Under the article's first passage rule each population is closed at its
own time and stays closed, so every population can have met its criterion
with part of the budget unspent. The same pilot data, carried on under
that rule:

```{r budget-closed}
set.seed(113)
scores_fp <- lapply(true_means, function(mu) {
  rnorm(seq_budget_pilot(m_0 = 10), mean = mu, sd = 8)
})

closed <- NULL
repeat {
  out_fp <- seq_budget(scores_fp, weights, cost_per_group = costs,
                       budget = budget, closed = closed)
  closed <- attr(out_fp, "met_per_group")
  g <- seq_budget_next(out_fp, order = "rounds")
  if (is.na(g)) break
  scores_fp[[g]] <- c(scores_fp[[g]], rnorm(1, mean = true_means[g], sd = 8))
}
attr(out_fp, "n_per_group")
c(rule_met = attr(out_fp, "rule_met"),
  budget_exhausted = attr(out_fp, "budget_exhausted"))
attr(out_fp, "remaining_budget")
```

```{r budget-closed-text, include = FALSE}
fp_ending <- if (attr(out_fp, "rule_met")) {
  "with every population closed"
} else {
  "by exhaustion as well"
}
```

This run ended `r fp_ending`, with
`r f(attr(out_fp, "remaining_budget"), 0)` of the budget unspent
(`r f(attr(out, "remaining_budget"), 0)` under the default). In
`r tour_G_text` simulated studies of the design under the first passage
rule (`procedure = "first_passage"` in `seq_budget_sensitivity()`),
`r f(tour_value("budget_first_passage", "pct_rule_met"), 1)`% ended with
every population closed. The mean cost was
`r f(tour_value("budget_first_passage", "mean_total_cost"), 0)`, against
`r f(tour_value("budget", "mean_total_cost"), 0)` under the default, and
the 95% interval covered the contrast in
`r f(100 * tour_value("budget_first_passage", "coverage"), 1)`% of
studies, against `r f(100 * tour_value("budget", "coverage"), 1)`%. The
option is the package's reading of the article's sequence, not a step for
step copy of it; the help page of `seq_budget_next()` sets out three
details that differ.

The interval from the default run `r contains(out, -1)` the true contrast
of −1. Like the others in this vignette, its coverage is asymptotic. In
the simulated studies of the default procedure,
`r f(tour_value("budget", "pct_within_budget"), 0)`% ended within the
budget, and the estimated variance of the contrast averaged
`r f(tour_value("budget", "mean_estimated_variance"), 3)` where the true
variance at the final sample sizes averaged
`r f(tour_value("budget", "mean_true_variance"), 3)`. A variance estimate
that runs low is what costs coverage in a small study. A smaller budget or
a very small pilot costs more; the help page of `seq_budget_pilot()` has
the figures.

### Noninferiority and Equivalence

The article's purpose is a decision. Its noninferiority test asks whether
any shortfall of the online module against the instructor-led formats is
smaller than a margin, here 4 points. The null hypothesis is inferiority
(the contrast is at or below −4), and at one-sided level 0.05 it is
rejected when the estimate is more than 1.645 standard errors above −4.
Equivalence within 4 points either way is two such one-sided tests.

```{r budget-decide}
decide_seq_budget_noninferiority(out, margin = 4, alpha_level = 0.05)
decide_seq_budget_equivalence(out, margin_lower = -4, margin_upper = 4,
                              alpha_level = 0.05)
```

`TRUE` means the null hypothesis is rejected, so the conclusion named by
the function is supported; `FALSE` is not evidence for the null
hypothesis. In the simulated studies of this design, in which the online
module is truly one point worse, the noninferiority test with a margin of
4 rejected in
`r f(100 * tour_value("budget", "noninferiority_rejection_rate"), 1)`% of
them under the default and in
`r f(100 * tour_value("budget_first_passage", "noninferiority_rejection_rate"), 1)`%
under the first passage rule: that is its power here. The decisions use
the contrast estimate and its variance, with their own one-sided
`alpha_level`, not the two-sided limits printed on the check: a one-sided
test at 0.05 corresponds to a 90% interval. Code the contrast so that
larger values favor the treatment of interest, as here.
`decide_seq_budget_superiority()` and `decide_seq_budget_inferiority()`
test the contrast against a single margin from either side. The vignette
`vignette("seq-budget", package = "SMSD")` covers the procedure in full,
including the article's first passage rule and what to expect before the
study from `seq_budget_sensitivity()`.

## Minimum Risk Point Estimation

The procedures so far aim at a confidence interval. Minimum risk point
estimation aims at a point estimate and prices its error. An observation
costs *c*, a unit of squared estimation error costs *A*, and the sample
size that minimizes the expected total depends on unknown parameters, so
it is found sequentially. There is no confidence level and no interval.
The articles build *A* from what the researcher would pay to estimate the
parameter to within a chosen margin: that amount divided by the square of
the margin.

For the coefficient of variation (Chattopadhyay & Kelley, 2016), suppose
12,500 is the price of estimating κ to within 0.05, so
*A* = 12,500 / 0.05<sup>2</sup>, and an observation costs 10. The response
times are simulated from a gamma distribution with κ = 0.4.

```{r mr-cv}
set.seed(113)
A <- 12500 / 0.05^2
response_time <- rgamma(400, shape = 1 / 0.4^2, rate = 5)

seq_mr_cv_pilot(A = A, c = 10)
path_mr <- seq_path(seq_mr_cv, response_time, A = A, c = 10)
attr(path_mr, "stop_n")
attr(path_mr, "final_check")
```

The rows are the estimate, the estimated risk at the current sample size,
the variance estimate, and the criterion (`optimal_n`). In
`r tour_G_text` simulated studies with these constants and this
population, the mean final sample size was
`r f(tour_value("mr_cv", "ratio_n"), 2)` times the best fixed sample size
(`r f(tour_value("mr_cv", "optimal_n"), 0)`), and the realized risk was
`r f(tour_value("mr_cv", "risk_efficiency"), 2)` times the minimum. By
default
`seq_mr_cv()` uses the distribution free variance of the 2018 article,
which is consistent for data that are not normal; `variance = "published"`
gives Equation 22 of the 2016 article, for reproducing that article. The
vignette `vignette("mrpe-cv", package = "SMSD")` explains the difference.

For the standardized mean difference (Chattopadhyay & Kelley, 2017) the
check also reports the size each group should have at the next check
(`next_n1` and `next_n2`, which equal the current sizes once the rule is
met), and `c` may be a pair of costs when the two groups cost different
amounts.

```{r mr-smd}
set.seed(113)
treated <- rnorm(150, mean = 0.5)
untreated <- rnorm(150, mean = 0)

seq_mr_smd_pilot(A = 10000, c = 2.4)
path_mr2 <- seq_path(seq_mr_smd, list(group_1 = treated, group_2 = untreated),
                     A = 10000, c = 2.4)
attr(path_mr2, "final_check")
```

In `r tour_G_text` simulated studies with these constants, the mean final
sample size per group was `r f(tour_value("mr_smd", "ratio_n1"), 2)` times
the best fixed sample size
(`r f(tour_value("mr_smd", "optimal_n1"), 1)` per group), and the realized
risk was `r f(tour_value("mr_smd", "risk_efficiency"), 2)` times the
minimum. Both
procedures have sensitivity functions, `seq_mr_cv_sensitivity()` and
`seq_mr_smd_sensitivity()`, which make these comparisons. See
`vignette("mrpe-smd", package = "SMSD")` for the second procedure.

## Classical Procedures

The remaining functions implement procedures from Mukhopadhyay and de
Silva (2009) for a mean, for the location of a negative exponential
distribution, and for a median. They follow the same contract (a pilot
function, a check function, an `smsd_check` object).

| Goal | Functions |
|:---|:---|
| Confidence interval of fixed width for a mean, purely sequential | `seq_fwd_norm_mean()`, `seq_fwd_dfr_mean()` |
| The same in two stages | `ts_fwd_norm_mean()`, `ts_fwd_dfr_mean()` |
| Confidence interval of fixed width for a negative exponential location, purely sequential and in two stages | `seq_fwd_nexp_mean()`, `ts_fwd_nexp_mean()` |
| Minimum risk point estimation of a mean | `seq_mr_norm_mean()`, `seq_mr_exp_mean()`, `seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb()` |
| Minimum risk point estimation of a negative exponential location | `seq_mr_nexp_mean()` |
| Bounded risk point estimation of a mean | `seq_br_norm_mean()`, `ts_br_norm_mean()`, `ts_br_exp_mean()` |
| Confidence interval of bounded length for a median | `seq_blci_dfr_median()` |

In the names, `norm` is a normal population, `exp` an exponential one,
and `dfr` distribution free. The three `nexp` functions end in `mean`
like the others, but what they estimate is the location (the minimum) of
a negative exponential distribution, not its mean, which is the location
plus the scale. In the fixed width procedures for a normal or a
distribution free mean, the argument `d` is the half width of the interval
(the margin of error), not the full width that the `seq_aipe_*()` family
takes; each help page defines it.

Stein's (1945) two stage procedure shows the pattern. A first stage fixes
the total sample size, and one further sample completes it. A training
director wants the mean score on a 100 point assessment to within 2
points with 95% confidence.

```{r stein}
set.seed(113)
first_stage <- rnorm(ts_fwd_norm_mean_pilot(d = 2), mean = 70, sd = 8)
check <- ts_fwd_norm_mean(first_stage, d = 2)
attr(check, "criterion_n")

second_stage <- rnorm(attr(check, "criterion_n") - length(first_stage),
                      mean = 70, sd = 8)
ts_fwd_norm_mean(first_stage, second_stage, d = 2)
```

For normal data this interval covers the mean with probability at least
the confidence level at any first stage size, a guarantee that is exact
rather than asymptotic; the price is a larger expected sample size than a
known variance would need. The guarantees of the other classical
procedures differ, some exact and some asymptotic, and each help page
states which, with measured figures.

The distribution free counterpart, `ts_fwd_dfr_mean()`, is the one whose
shortfall most needs to be known. It puts the first stage variance into
the known variance sample size with a normal quantile and no allowance
for having estimated it, so its confidence level is reached only as the
first stage grows. For normal data and a narrow target its coverage is
the probability that a *t* variable, with degrees of freedom one less
than the first stage size, falls between −*z* and *z*:

```{r dfr-coverage}
first_stage_size <- c(10, 30, 100)
coverage <- 2 * pt(qnorm(0.975), df = first_stage_size - 1) - 1
round(setNames(coverage, first_stage_size), 3)
```

These are below the nominal 0.95 at every first stage size, and the help
page reports less for skewed data: with a first stage of 30, a population
standard deviation of 2, and `d = 0.2`, coverage was 0.915 for
exponential data and 0.874 for lognormal data. If the data can be taken
as normal, use Stein's procedure. If they cannot and only one further
round of data collection is possible, give the first stage as many
observations as the study allows. The vignette
`vignette("special-cases-and-simulation", package = "SMSD")` discusses
the classical procedures.
<!-- figures from `?ts_fwd_dfr_mean` -->

A few helpers complete the package. `gini_index()`, `gini_mean_diff()`,
and `slr_slope()` return point estimates used above;
`seq_fwd_norm_mean_optimal()` gives the sample size a fixed width interval
for a normal mean would need if the variance were known; and `power_z()`
gives the Type II error and the sample size of a one sample, one-sided
*z* test.

## Before Any Data: The Sensitivity Functions

The figures given above for each design, and those quoted from the help
pages, were obtained by simulating the whole procedure, pilot to stopping
point, many times against a population with a known value. The sensitivity
functions do that in one call, and they are the way to learn what a
planned study should expect: how large the sample is likely to become, how
variable that is, and what coverage the interval has at the planned
width.

The argument `batch` is the number of observations added between checks.
The default of 1 is the purely sequential procedure. A study that can
check only after every 10 participants per group stops later than the
first sample size at which the rule would have been met. For the design
of Method 1:

```{r sensitivity}
batched <- seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity(true_value = 0.5, width = 0.40, G = 100,
                                    seed = 113, batch = 10)
batched
```

```{r sensitivity-values, include = FALSE}
batched_mean_n <- value_of(batched, "mean_n")
batched_coverage <- value_of(batched, "coverage")
batched_se <- sqrt(batched_coverage * (1 - batched_coverage) / 100)
```

Checking after every 10 per group, the mean final sample size is
`r f(batched_mean_n, 1)` per group, against
`r f(smd_row(0.5)$mean_n, 1)` in the verification study, where the rule is
checked after every observation. The help page reports the same pattern
from larger runs: checking less often costs about half a batch per group.
One hundred replications say little about coverage (its Monte Carlo
standard error here is about `r f(batched_se, 2)`); a design decision
deserves several thousand. The vignette
`vignette("sensitivity-analysis", package = "SMSD")` treats these
functions in full.

## A Verification Study

A single run cannot show whether a procedure delivers what it promises.
The package therefore ships the results of a Monte Carlo study of two of
its procedures, the standardized mean difference and the Pearson
correlation, with `r G_text` replications in each of 18 conditions. Each
replication runs the shipped check function as a prospective study would:
the pilot sample, then one observation at a time (per group, or one pair),
with the rule checked after each, to the first check that is met. The
study is computed once and cached, because it takes hours of processor
time, and the vignette only reads it. The same file holds
`r tour_G_text` simulated studies of the design of each method section
from Method 3 on, run with the sensitivity functions, the budget design
of Method 9 under both readings of the procedure (the designs of Methods
1 and 2 are among the 18 conditions); they are tabulated below.

```{r load-sim}
sim <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "aipe_simulation_results.rds",
                           package = "SMSD"))
str(sim$meta[c("G", "conf_level", "seed", "generated_on", "smsd_version",
               "r_version")])
```

Two data generating mechanisms are used: normal data, and right skewed
data from a chi square distribution with 3 degrees of freedom,
standardized (skewness 1.63). Three results are reported for each
condition.

* **Coverage**: the proportion of final intervals that contain the true
  value. With `r G_text` replications, the Monte Carlo standard error of a
  coverage near 0.95 is `r f(sqrt(0.95 * 0.05 / meta$G), 4)`, and of one
  near 0.70 it is `r f(sqrt(0.70 * 0.30 / meta$G), 4)`.
* **Final width**: at most ω in every replication, by construction.
* **Final sample size**, beside *N*\*, the sample size that the true
  asymptotic variance would require, ⌈(2*z* / ω)<sup>2</sup>
  ξ<sup>2</sup>⌉ (2018, Equation 20; 2019, Equation 7). A procedure that
  estimates ξ<sup>2</sup> well stops near *N*\*.

```{r width-check, include = FALSE}
width_text <- if (all(s$pct_width_le_omega == 100)) {
  "every replication of every condition"
} else {
  "fewer than all replications (column pct_width_le_omega of the summary)"
}
cap_text <- if (all(s$pct_hit_max_n == 0)) {
  "no replication reached"
} else {
  "some replications reached"
}
```

The width requirement held in `r width_text`, and `r cap_text` the cap of
`r f(meta$max_n, 0)` on the sample size.

### The Standardized Mean Difference

```{r sim-smd-table, echo = FALSE}
smd <- s[s$method == "Standardized mean difference", ]
smd_table <- data.frame(
  smd$true_value, smd$distribution, smd$theoretical_n, f(smd$mean_n, 1),
  f(smd$sd_n, 1), f(smd$mean_width, 3), f(smd$coverage, 3)
)
names(smd_table) <- c("True \u03b4", "Data", "N*", "Mean N", "SD of N",
                      "Mean width", "Coverage")
knitr::kable(
  smd_table,
  row.names = FALSE, align = "rlrrrrr",
  caption = paste0("Sequential AIPE for the standardized mean difference at ",
                   "a target width of 0.40 and a 95% level: ", G_text,
                   " replications per row. Sample sizes are per group.")
)
```

```{r sim-smd-values, include = FALSE}
smd_n <- smd[smd$distribution == "normal", ]
smd_k <- smd[smd$distribution == "skewed", ]
se_cov <- function(p) sqrt(p * (1 - p) / meta$G)
z_n <- (smd_n$coverage - 0.95) / se_cov(smd_n$coverage)
z_k <- (0.95 - smd_k$coverage) / se_cov(smd_k$coverage)
```

For normal data coverage was `r f(min(smd_n$coverage), 3)` to
`r f(max(smd_n$coverage), 3)`, never more than `r f(max(abs(z_n)), 1)`
Monte Carlo standard errors from 0.95, and the mean final sample size was
within `r f(max(abs(smd_n$mean_n - smd_n$theoretical_n)), 1)` of *N*\* in
every row. For the skewed data coverage was
`r f(min(smd_k$coverage), 3)` to `r f(max(smd_k$coverage), 3)`: below
0.95 in all three rows, by `r f(min(z_k), 1)` to `r f(max(z_k), 1)`
standard errors, and by `r f(100 * (0.95 - mean(smd_k$coverage)), 1)` of
a percentage point on average. That shortfall is small, and with this
many replications it is more than Monte Carlo error. Under skew the final
sample size is also more variable, and its mean was
`r f(min(smd_k$theoretical_n - smd_k$mean_n), 1)` to
`r f(max(smd_k$theoretical_n - smd_k$mean_n), 1)` per group below *N*\*,
the larger the effect the further below. No variance estimate was unusable
in any replication of these six conditions.

```{r sim-smd-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.6, fig.alt = "Two histograms of the final sample size per group for a standardized mean difference of 0.5 at a target width of 0.40. Left: normal data, a narrow distribution centered at N*. Right: skewed data, a wider distribution centered slightly below N*.", fig.cap = "Final sample size per group for δ = 0.5 at a target width of 0.40, for normal data (left) and skewed data (right). The dashed line marks *N*\\*."}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
rng <- range(sim$spotlight$smd_normal$n, sim$spotlight$smd_skewed$n)
for (key in c("smd_normal", "smd_skewed")) {
  sp <- sim$spotlight[[key]]
  hist(sp$n, breaks = seq(rng[1] - 0.5, rng[2] + 4.5, by = 5), xlim = rng,
       col = "gray85", border = "white", xlab = "Final n per group",
       main = if (key == "smd_normal") "Normal data" else "Skewed data")
  abline(v = sp$theoretical_n, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
}
par(op)
```

Both groups have the same shape in these conditions, so the corrected and
the printed form of Equation 26 agree in the population, and this study
is not evidence about the correction. That evidence is the derivation in
the correction note and the package's tests of the variance estimator.

### The Pearson Correlation

The table sweeps the target width at each true correlation, for normal
data. The last two columns give the percentage of replications in which
the variance estimate was unusable (zero or negative) at one or more
checks, so that sampling continued past a check the printed rule would
have ended on, and the percentage that ended with the bound
*n*<sup>−3</sup> standing in for a smaller positive estimate, as the
articles prescribe.

```{r sim-cor-table, echo = FALSE}
cor_tab <- s[s$method == "Pearson correlation" & s$distribution == "normal", ]
cor_tab <- cor_tab[order(cor_tab$true_value, -cor_tab$width), ]
cor_table <- data.frame(
  cor_tab$true_value, f(cor_tab$width, 2), cor_tab$pilot_n,
  f(cor_tab$theoretical_n, 0), f(cor_tab$mean_n, 1),
  f(cor_tab$mean_width, 3), f(cor_tab$coverage, 3),
  f(cor_tab$pct_variance_unusable, 1), f(cor_tab$pct_bound_stop, 2)
)
names(cor_table) <- c("True \u03c1", "Target width", "Pilot", "N*", "Mean N",
                      "Mean width", "Coverage", "Unusable (%)", "Bound (%)")
knitr::kable(
  cor_table,
  row.names = FALSE, align = "r",
  caption = paste0("Sequential AIPE for the Pearson correlation, normal ",
                   "data, 95% level: ", G_text, " replications per row.")
)
```

```{r sim-cor-values, include = FALSE}
wide <- cor_tab[cor_tab$width == 0.30, ]
mid <- cor_tab[cor_tab$width == 0.15, ]
fine <- cor_tab[cor_tab$width == 0.08, ]
fine_07 <- fine$coverage[fine$true_value == 0.7]
z_fine_07 <- (0.95 - fine_07) / se_cov(fine_07)
```

Read each block from top to bottom. At ω = 0.30 the procedure stops with
`r f(min(wide$mean_n), 0)` to `r f(max(wide$mean_n), 0)` pairs on average
and coverage is `r f(min(wide$coverage), 3)` to
`r f(max(wide$coverage), 3)`, lowest for the strongest correlation. At
ω = 0.15 it is `r f(min(mid$coverage), 3)` to `r f(max(mid$coverage), 3)`,
and at ω = 0.08, where the final samples hold
`r f(min(fine$mean_n), 0)` to `r f(max(fine$mean_n), 0)` pairs on average,
`r f(min(fine$coverage), 3)` to `r f(max(fine$coverage), 3)`: within about
a percentage point of the confidence level, and for ρ = 0.7 still
`r f(z_fine_07, 1)` standard errors short of it. The mean final sample size is below *N*\* in
every row, by a larger share at wide targets: the rule is first met when
the variance estimate happens to be low, and that is when the interval is
too narrow.

```{r sim-cor-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "Coverage against the mean final number of pairs, on a logarithmic axis, for true correlations of 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7. Coverage is far below 0.95 at the smallest mean sample sizes and close to it at the largest; the line for 0.7 is lowest.", fig.cap = "Coverage of the 95% interval for the Pearson correlation against the mean final sample size, for normal data. Each line joins the three target widths (0.30, 0.15, 0.08) at one true correlation. The dashed line is the confidence level."}
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
rhos <- sort(unique(cor_tab$true_value))
plot(NA, xlim = range(cor_tab$mean_n), ylim = c(min(cor_tab$coverage), 1),
     log = "x", xlab = "Mean final number of pairs (log scale)",
     ylab = "Coverage")
abline(h = 0.95, lty = 2)
for (j in seq_along(rhos)) {
  block <- cor_tab[cor_tab$true_value == rhos[j], ]
  block <- block[order(block$mean_n), ]
  lines(block$mean_n, block$coverage, type = "b", pch = c(15, 16, 17)[j],
        lty = j, lwd = 2)
}
legend("bottomright", legend = paste("rho =", rhos), pch = c(15, 16, 17),
       lty = seq_along(rhos), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
par(op)
```

```{r sim-wide-values, include = FALSE}
sp <- sim$spotlight$cor_wide
early <- sp$n <= 2 * sp$pilot_n
```

The wide target for ρ = 0.7 shows the mechanism. The pilot is
`r sim$spotlight$cor_wide$pilot_n` pairs and *N*\* is
`r sim$spotlight$cor_wide$theoretical_n`. Of the `r G_text` replications,
`r f(100 * mean(early), 1)`% stopped with no more than
`r 2 * sp$pilot_n` pairs, and their intervals covered ρ
`r f(100 * mean(sp$covered[early]), 1)`% of the time; the replications
that ran longer covered it `r f(100 * mean(sp$covered[!early]), 1)`% of
the time. Of the intervals that missed,
`r f(100 * mean(early[!sp$covered]), 0)`% came from those early stops.

The package's rule for an unusable variance estimate matters most in these
conditions. In the `r f(wide$pct_variance_unusable[wide$true_value == 0.7], 1)`%
of replications for ρ = 0.7 at ω = 0.30 in which the estimate was zero or
negative at some check, the rule as printed would have stopped there with
an interval of nearly zero width. Requiring a usable estimate removes
those stops; it does not make the remaining early stops trustworthy, as
the coverage column shows. The few replications that ended with the bound
in place of a small positive estimate
(`r f(wide$pct_bound_stop[wide$true_value == 0.7], 2)`% in the same
condition) have that near zero width too, and are what the articles'
rule prescribes.

At the narrowest width the procedure was also run with the skewed data.

```{r sim-cor-skew, echo = FALSE}
sk <- s[s$method == "Pearson correlation" & s$distribution == "skewed", ]
sk <- sk[order(sk$true_value), ]
skew_table <- data.frame(
  sk$true_value, f(sk$width, 2), f(sk$theoretical_n, 0), f(sk$mean_n, 1),
  f(sk$sd_n, 1), f(sk$coverage, 3), f(sk$pct_variance_unusable, 1)
)
names(skew_table) <- c("True \u03c1", "Target width", "N*", "Mean N",
                       "SD of N", "Coverage", "Unusable (%)")
knitr::kable(
  skew_table,
  row.names = FALSE, align = "r",
  caption = paste0("Sequential AIPE for the Pearson correlation, skewed ",
                   "data, 95% level: ", G_text, " replications per row.")
)
```

Skewed data need more pairs for the same width (compare *N*\* with the
normal rows), and the procedure, which is not told the shape, collects
most of them: the mean final sample size is
`r f(min(100 * (1 - sk$mean_n / sk$theoretical_n)), 1)`% to
`r f(max(100 * (1 - sk$mean_n / sk$theoretical_n)), 1)`% below *N*\*.
Coverage at this width is `r f(min(sk$coverage), 3)` to
`r f(max(sk$coverage), 3)`, lowest again for ρ = 0.7.

### The Designs of the Method Sections

Each example in this vignette is one run. The table gives the long run
behavior of the same designs. Methods 1 and 2 are rows of the tables
above; the others were simulated with the calls listed below the table.

```{r sim-tour-table, echo = FALSE}
budget_n <- tour_value("budget", "mean_n_1") +
  tour_value("budget", "mean_n_2") + tour_value("budget", "mean_n_3")
budget_fp_n <- tour_value("budget_first_passage", "mean_n_1") +
  tour_value("budget_first_passage", "mean_n_2") +
  tour_value("budget_first_passage", "mean_n_3")
tour_table <- data.frame(
  c(1:9, 9),
  c("Standardized mean difference", "Pearson correlation",
    "Squared multiple correlation", "Coefficient of variation",
    "Regression slope", "Standardized mean", "Contrast", "Gini index",
    "Contrast under a budget, default",
    "Contrast under a budget, first passage rule"),
  c(G_text, G_text, rep(tour_G_text, 8)),
  f(c(smd_row(0.5)$mean_n, cor_row(0.5, 0.15)$mean_n,
      tour_value("R2", "mean_n"), tour_value("cv", "mean_n"),
      tour_value("reg_coef", "mean_n"), tour_value("sm", "mean_n"),
      tour_value("contrast", "mean_n"), tour_value("gini", "mean_n"),
      budget_n, budget_fp_n), 1),
  f(c(smd_row(0.5)$coverage, cor_row(0.5, 0.15)$coverage,
      tour_value("R2", "coverage"), tour_value("cv", "coverage"),
      tour_value("reg_coef", "coverage"), tour_value("sm", "coverage"),
      tour_value("contrast", "coverage"), tour_value("gini", "coverage"),
      tour_value("budget", "coverage"),
      tour_value("budget_first_passage", "coverage")), 3)
)
names(tour_table) <- c("Method", "Effect size", "Simulated studies",
                       "Mean final n", "Coverage")
knitr::kable(
  tour_table, row.names = FALSE, align = "rlrrr",
  caption = paste0("The design of each method section, at a 95% level. ",
                   "The mean final sample size is per group for Methods 1 ",
                   "and 7 and the total over the three groups for Method 9.")
)
```

```{r tour-calls}
writeLines(strwrap(sim$tour$calls, width = 76, exdent = 4))
```

```{r sim-tour-values, include = FALSE}
tour_cov <- c(tour_value("R2", "coverage"), tour_value("cv", "coverage"),
              tour_value("reg_coef", "coverage"), tour_value("sm", "coverage"),
              tour_value("contrast", "coverage"),
              tour_value("budget", "coverage"),
              tour_value("budget_first_passage", "coverage"))
tour_se <- sqrt(0.95 * 0.05 / tour[["G"]])
```

With `r tour_G_text` studies, the Monte Carlo standard error of a coverage
near 0.95 is `r f(tour_se, 4)`. Apart from the Gini index, the designs
simulated here cover between `r f(min(tour_cov), 3)` and
`r f(max(tour_cov), 3)`; the Gini index for lognormal data at ω = 0.10,
where the final samples hold about
`r f(tour_value("gini", "mean_n"), 0)` observations, covers
`r f(tour_value("gini", "coverage"), 3)`.

### What the Study Says, and What It Does Not

The width guarantee is exact and held without exception. The coverage
guarantee is a statement about narrow targets, and how narrow depends on
the effect size. For the standardized mean difference a width of 0.40,
reached with `r f(min(smd$mean_n), 0)` to `r f(max(smd$mean_n), 0)` per
group on average, is narrow enough for coverage within a percentage point
of the confidence level: it was between
`r f(100 * min(smd$coverage), 1)`% and `r f(100 * max(smd$coverage), 1)`%
in all six conditions, at the confidence level for normal data and about
half a percentage point below it for the skewed data. For the Pearson
correlation a width of 0.30, which looks reasonable, gives intervals that
cover the true value in `r f(100 * min(wide$coverage), 0)`% to
`r f(100 * max(wide$coverage), 0)`% of studies, not 95%, and a strong
correlation needs a narrower target than a moderate one. The remedy is in
the user's hands: a narrower width, a larger minimum pilot sample size,
and a sensitivity analysis at the strongest plausible value before the
study begins (Maxwell, Kelley, & Rausch, 2008, discuss planning for
accuracy more broadly).

The 18 conditions cover two effect sizes at a 95% level under two data
generating mechanisms. For the other procedures the file holds one design
each, the one of its method section, which is evidence about that design
and no other. Their measured coverage under further conditions (wider
targets, skewed data, stronger relationships, more predictors) is on
their help pages and is quoted in the sections above.

### Reproducing the Study

The script that produced the cached file is `simulation_study.R` in the
`data-raw` folder of the package's source repository,
<https://github.com/yelleKneK/SMSD>. That folder is not part of the
installed package. The script calls `seq_aipe_smd()` and `seq_aipe_r()`
after every observation, checks before the long run that its loop
reproduces `seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity()` and `seq_aipe_r_sensitivity()`
exactly for the same seed, and fixes the seed of every block of
`r f(meta$chunk_size, 0)` replications (a chunk, in the script and in
`sim$meta`), so the results do not depend on the number of processes. It
is run from the package's source directory with
`Rscript data-raw/simulation_study.R`, after the package has been
installed; the environment variable `SMSD_SIM_CORES` sets the number of
processes.

```{r run-time, include = FALSE}
timing <- meta[["timing"]]
narrow <- which(s$method == "Pearson correlation" & s$width == 0.08)
narrow_share <- sum(timing$cpu_seconds[timing$condition %in% narrow]) /
  sum(timing$cpu_seconds)
machine <- if (is.na(meta[["cpu"]])) {
  paste("the platform", meta[["platform"]])
} else {
  paste0("a computer with the processor ", meta[["cpu"]], " (",
         meta[["platform"]], ")")
}
```

The run that produced this file took `r f(meta$cpu_hours, 1)` hours of
processor time for the 18 conditions,
`r f(100 * narrow_share, 0)`% of it in the six correlation conditions at
ω = 0.08, and a further `r f(meta$tour_cpu_minutes, 0)` minutes for the
designs of the method sections. Spread over `r meta$cores` processes, the
18 conditions took `r f(meta$wall_minutes, 0)` minutes of elapsed time.
The run was made on `r machine`, under `r meta$r_version`, with SMSD
`r meta$smsd_version`; the file is dated `r meta$generated_on`.

Any row can also be checked from the installed package alone, with the
matching sensitivity function. The conditions are numbered as the rows of
`sim$summary`, which the tables above sort differently. Block *j* of
condition *i* was run under the seed `r meta$seed` + 1000*i* + *j*, and it
is exactly what the sensitivity function returns for that seed with `G`
set to `r meta$chunk_size`. To keep this vignette quick to build, the
chunk below finds the condition for ρ = 0.7 at ω = 0.30 and runs the
first 50 replications of its first block:

```{r one-block}
i <- with(sim$summary, which(method == "Pearson correlation" &
                               distribution == "normal" &
                               true_value == 0.7 & width == 0.30))
c(condition = i, seed = sim$meta$seed + 1000 * i + 1)
seq_aipe_r_sensitivity(true_value = 0.7, width = 0.30, G = 50,
                       seed = sim$meta$seed + 1000 * i + 1)
```

With another seed, or more replications, the same call checks the row
within Monte Carlo error. The designs of the method sections were run in
the same way, in blocks of `r f(meta$chunk_size, 0)`: block *j* of the
*k*th call listed above is that call with `G` set to
`r meta$chunk_size` and `seed` set to
`r as.integer(meta$seed + 100000)` + 1000*k* + *j*.

## Relationship to DMAR

`SMSD` is the sequential complement of `DMAR`, which is on CRAN and is
loaded with `SMSD`. When a planning value is trusted, `DMAR` gives the
sample size at once. For the design of Method 1, had δ = 0.5 been known:

```{r dmar}
print(ss_aipe_smd(delta = 0.5, width = 0.40))
```

The sequential procedure was not told δ and stopped at
`r attr(path, "stop_n")` per group in the run above, and at
`r f(smd_row(0.5)$mean_n, 1)` per group on average in the verification
study. The fixed sample size planners `ss_aipe_r()`,
`ss_aipe_R2()`, `ss_aipe_cv()`, `ss_aipe_reg_coef()`, `ss_aipe_sm()`, and
`ss_aipe_c()` in `DMAR` are the counterparts of Methods 2 to 7; the Gini
index has no counterpart there. If the sample size can be fixed honestly,
fix it; otherwise let the data decide.

## Reproducibility

Every example above that draws random numbers starts from seed 113, set
with `set.seed(113)` or passed as the `seed` argument, so the code of each
section can be run by itself. (The one block reproduced from the
verification study uses that block's seed.) The examples are single
runs: an interval that contains the value used to generate the data
illustrates the procedure and proves nothing about it, and at a 95% level
about one such interval in twenty should miss. The evidence about
coverage is the verification study and the simulations reported on the
help pages.
